questions.title: How does the KL‑constrained optimal policy in DPO differ from the standard REINFORCE policy used in PPO?
questions.question_body:
The paper derives the optimal policy for a reward function with a KL constraint as 
$$\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\bigl(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\bigr).$$
I understand this is a soft‑max reweighting of the reference policy, but I am confused how this differs from the actor‑critic style updates used in PPO. Does the KL term guarantee the same behaviour? Also, why is the partition function $Z(x)$ problematic to estimate, and why does DPO avoid it altogether?

questions.title: Why does reparameterizing the reward as $r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ preserve all reward classes?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that every reward class can be represented with this log‑ratio form for some policy π. I follow that adding a constant to all rewards leaves preferences unchanged, but how does this specific choice of $r$ ensure that we can recover *any* reward function within the equivalence class? In particular, what role does the reference policy play, and could we pick a different reference and still represent the same class?

questions.title: What intuition lies behind the importance weight $σ(	ilde r_θ(y_l)−	ilde r_θ(y_w))$ in the DPO gradient?
questions.question_body:
In Equation (12) the gradient contains a sigmoid term $
abla_θ  igl[σ(	ilde r_θ(y_l)−	ilde r_θ(y_w)) igr]$ that scales how much we adjust $	heta$ for a given preference pair. I get that it gives more weight when the model’s implicit reward disagrees with human preference, but could you explain in concrete terms how this weight prevents degeneration? Also, how sensitive is DPO to choosing $ eta$ that sets this weighting scale?

questions.title: How is a reference policy π_ref chosen when no SFT model exists?
questions.question_body: When working with datasets where no supervised fine‑tuned model is available (e.g., Anthropic helpful‑harmless dialogue), the paper proposes initializing $\,π_{	ext{ref}}$ by maximizing likelihood over preferred completions. How does this differ from simply using a vanilla pre‑trained LM, and why is it important for mitigating distribution shift? Are there scenarios where this strategy might fail?

questions.title: Why does DPO outperform PPO even when PPO has access to ground‑truth rewards?
questions.question_body: Figure 4 shows DPO achieving higher reward–KL frontiers than PPO (and even PPO‐GT). Intuitively I would expect an RL algorithm with an oracle reward to outperform a direct preference optimisation method. Could you unpack what gives DPO this advantage? Is it purely due to better optimisation dynamics or something inherent in modelling preferences via Bradley‑Terry?

questions.title: Can you walk through an example of deriving Equation (8) from Equation (7) by canceling the partition function?
questions.question_body: Equation (7) expresses human preferences via a Bradley‑Terry model using rewards derived from Eq (6). The paper then simplifies to Eq (8), where $Z(x)$ disappears. Could you provide a step‑by‑step derivation showing exactly how $Z(x)$ cancels and why it only depends on $x$? This would help me understand why preferences only depend on ratios of policies.

questions.title: How does DPO handle multi‑way rankings beyond pairwise comparisons?
questions.question_body: The theoretical derivation relies on Bradley‑Terry pairwise preference models. In practice some datasets contain full rankings of several completions per prompt. Is DPO directly applicable to such Plackett‑Luce data, or do we need extra preprocessing? What changes would appear in Equation (9) if we had more than two items?

questions.title: "Unlikelihood" vs. DPO: What causes unlikelihood training to degenerate when $ eta=0$?
questions.question_body:
The paper mentions that removing the weight term (i.e., setting $ eta=0$) leads to degeneracy as shown in Appendix Table X. Why does unlikelihood training collapse in this scenario? Is it because it maximises $
abla  igl[
abla 	ext{log} π(y_w)-
abla 	ext{log} π(y_l) igr]$ without any check on whether the model already prefers $y_w$? Any intuition for why square‐error style penalties fail here?

questions.title: "Maximising log probability ratio" – Is this equivalent to using a language model as both policy and reward?
questions.question_body: "Your language model is secretly a reward model" claims that our policy implicitly defines a reward via $\hat r_θ(x,y)=β \log \frac{π_θ}{π_{ref}}$. Does this mean that at convergence $\,π_θ=π^*$ and thus $\,ℎ̂r$ matches ground truth? Can we practically compute $ĥr(x,y)$ during training and use it as an explicit reward for other algorithms?
